title.narrative: Ipas Access to Safe Abortion II
Ipas Access to Safe Abortion II

description.narrative:
Ipas is an internationally recognized NGO that works to advance reproductive justice by expanding access to safe abortion and contraception globally since 50 years back. Over the years, more than 69 000 women and adolescent girls have accessed safe abortion services and 53 000 have received post¬abortion contraception services.
The project has four key objectives that will be achieved before end of 2027: 1. Women and girls have improved access to available, accessible, and acceptable abortion, contraceptive, and SGBV services within Mozambique's health sector. 2. Humanitarian agencies have enhanced capacity to take evidence¬based action to protect SRHR before, during, and after humanitarian crises. 3. Communities reduce the prevalence of harmful gender norms and cultural practices, increase support for SRHR, and refer people to safe SRH services. 4. A national movement for SRHR—led primarily by women and young people— demands accountability from government leaders on SRHR and SGBV, and resists threats to progress.
This will be achieved through advocacy work in various forums, technical support, dialogue with target groups and local communities, training of health staff and upgrading of care facilities.
It is proposed to support a contribution of 190 million SEK during 2023¬2027 of which 98 million SEK will be allocated to Ipas for their programmatic work to achieve goals 1-3, 90 Million SEK to strengthen an established network of local civil society organizations working within the SRHR sphere, including LGBTQI issues, reflected in goal 4 above and 2 Million SEK for midterm review.

Ipas är en internationellt erkänd SRHR¬organisation som sedan 50 år tillbaka arbetar globalt med sexuell och reproduktiv hälsa och rättigheter och tillgång till säkra aborter. Under projektet har mer än 69 000 kvinnor och tonårsflickor fått tillgång till säkra aborter och 53 000 har fått preventivmedel efter abort.
Insatsen har följande mål som förväntas uppnås till 2027: 1. Kvinnor och barn har förbättrad tillgång till säkra aborter, preventivmedel och stödinsatser för sexuellt och könsbaserat våld inom hälso¬ och sjukvårdssystemet i Moçambique. 2. Humanitära aktörer har ökad kapacitet att vidta evidens¬baserade åtgärder för att skydda och tillförsäkra tillgång till SRHR före, i samband med samt efter konfliktrelaterade kriser. 3. Lokalsamhällen har bidragit till att minska omfattningen av skadliga könsrelaterade normer och beteenden, öka förståelsen kring SRHR och hänvisa människor till inrättningar som erbjuder säkra och tillförlitliga SRHR¬tjänster. 4. En nationell SRHR-rörelse, huvudsakligen ledd av kvinnor och ungdomar, som ställer krav på ett rättvist ansvarstagande från regering och myndigheter kring SRHR och sexuellt och könsbaserat våld och som kan stå emot hot mot progressiva framsteg inom SRHR¬ området.
Detta ska uppnås genom påverkansarbete inom olika forum, tekniskt stöd, dialog med målgrupper och lokalsamhällen, utbildning av hälsopersonal och uppgradering av vårdinrättningar.
Totalt föreslås ett stöd på 190 MSEK under åren 2023–2027 varav 98 MSEK fördelas till Ipas för att genomföra verksamhet som leder till ovanstående mål 1-3; 90 MSEK till att stärka ett etablerat nätverk av lokala civilsamhällsorganisationer som arbetar med SRHR, inklusive HBTQI¬frågor, i enlighet med ovan nämnda mål 4; samt 2 MSEK för en halvtidsöversyn.

The primary goal of the project is to build lasting momentum for gender equality and human rights in Mozambique through improved access to and respect for sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR), including safe abortion.
Objective 1: Women and girls have improved access to available, accessible, and acceptable abortion, contraceptive, and SGBV services within Mozambique's health sector
Objective 2: Humanitarian agencies have enhanced capacity to take evidence-based action to protect SRHR before, during, and after humanitarian crises
Objective 3: Communities reduce the prevalence of harmful gender norms and cultural practices, increase support for SRHR, and refer people to safe SRH services
Objective 4: A national movement for SRHR led primarily by women and young people demands accountability from government leaders on SRHR and SGBV, and resists threats to progress

title.narrative: Agreement Ipas Access to safe abortion II
Decision on contribution Ipas access to safe abortion II

description.narrative:
This contribution was approved in September 2023, considered year 1(Y1) of project implementation and inception period. 2024 (Y2) was the first full year of implementation.
The results below, contribute to Strategy objectives 2.2 Increased gender equality, including access to, and respect for, sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) and 1.2 Enhanced adaptability and strengthened resilience to climate change, and environmental and natural disasters of Strategy for Swedens development cooperation with Mozambique 20222026:
Objective 1: Women and girls have improved access to available, acceptable, and high-quality abortion, contraceptive, and SGBV services within Mozambique's health sector
• In 2024 alone, 19,938 abortion-related cases were recorded, of which 10,709 (54%) were post abortion care (PAC) and 9,229 (46%) were induced abortions. Nampula accounted for 58% of all cases, followed by Zambezia (41%) and Niassa (1%). This geographic distribution reflects disparities in health system capacity and programmatic maturity across provinces. In 2024, 57% of abortion cases involved women under 25, totaling 12,304 cases. • In 2024, 83% of women who received abortion care adopted at least one contraceptive method. Implants accounted for the majority (59%), followed by oral contraceptives (9%) and injectables 9%). However, the uptake of new health facilities remains below 65%, highlighting disparities in service quality and integration • Regarding GBV services in 2024, the health areas in which Ipas supports reported a total of 9,675 cases. Of these, 4,292 (44.4%) were cases of psychological violence, 3,230 (33.4%) cases of physical violence and 2,153 (22.3%) cases of sexual violence. • To address the immediate shortage in the province of Nampula, where a prolonged stock shortage was reported, Ipas purchased and distributed abortion medicinesMisoprostol and Mifepristone (6,498 units) and Misoprostol (1,908 units)to ensure the continuous provision of CAC for women and girls in the health facilities supported by the project. • Ipas actively participated in revising the national clinical guidelines on Comprehensive Abortion Care (CAC). These updates maintain the legal framework for abortion but introduce progressive measures such as: community-level abortion services in humanitarian settings; support for self-managed abortion; and Integration of abortion services into Mozambiques telemedicine strategy. • A new standardized consent form for abortion services was disseminated by the Ministry of Health. This includes enabling the appointment of a guardian on behalf of patients under 16 years of age to facilitate access to abortion services at health facilities. • A total of 59 health professionals (13 men and 46 women) participated in targeted training sessions, including provincial trainers for Comprehensive Abortion Care (CAC), provincial chief doctors, and obstetrician-gynecologists from all the provinces. These training sessions played a critical role in updating clinical protocols for induced abortion treatment and post-abortion care, ensuring alignment with the latest evidence-based practices. Additionally, the training introduced abortion management in humanitarian settings through community health workers, strengthened self-managed abortion approaches, and supported the integration of abortion services into the countrys telemedicine system. • Ipas is advancing telemedicine as an innovative way to expand access to safe, evidence-based SRH services, including abortion, contraception, and GBV support. A feasibility study with AMOG and the Central Hospital of Quelimane in Zambezia identified opportunities for using tele-consultations to support health care providers. During the reporting period, activities implemented also included stakeholder mapping, training, and infrastructure planning. The strategy also supports abortion self-care through collaboration with pharmacists and community health workers (CHWs). • On March 8 (International Womens Day), Ipas launched the WhatsApp-based chatbot Nurse Nina in Niassa. The chatbot is built upon the successful experiences of similar projects across various Ipas offices and was developed to expand the spaces providing information about SRHR and GBV, ultimately enabling girls, women, boys and men to make informed decisions and choices within these areas. The chatbot is WhatsApp-based, providing quick automatic responses that allow users to anonymously access the information. During the reporting period, 15,228 users accessed the Nina nursery platform. Of these, 13,489 users (89%) identified their gender, 10,028 (66%) were female and 3,461 (23%) were male. The largest user group by age was 2024 years, representing 38% of total users underscoring strong engagement from young people, especially young women.
Objective 2: Humanitarian agencies have enhanced capacity to take evidence-based action to protect SRHR before, during, and after humanitarian crises
• As part of this objective, actions aim to ensure that SRHR services, particularly those related to safe abortion care (CAC) and gender-based violence (SGBV), are accessible and effective in humanitarian settings, both before, during, and after crises. Key milestones included the initiation of mapping strategic partners for SRHR and climate resilience, identifying gaps in the integration of SGBV, SRHR, and safe abortion services in the humanitarian response, and adapting training packages to improve community health workers' capacity in these areas. • Despite these efforts, the implementation of some planned activities faced significant challenges. The socio-political context, particularly the post-election tensions and associated unrest, created an environment unsuitable for conducting sensitive activities, such as the Value Clarification and Attitude Transformation (VCAT) workshops. While some planned activities experienced delays or adjustmentssuch as the research on SRHR and climate resilience, as well as the Value Clarification and Attitude Transformation (VCAT) workshop strategic efforts have been made to adapt to these challenges. • Additionally, efforts to integrate and revitalize multisectoral humanitarian emergency response groups, as well as actions aimed at combating stigma, were postponed to Year 3 (Y3) due to these circumstances.
Objective 3: Communities reduce the prevalence of harmful gender norms and cultural practices, increase support for SRHR, and refer people to safe SRH services
• Ipas participated in 3 marches, 13 health fairs, and 3 road shows across three provinces, reaching approximately 5,500 people. These events were organized in collaboration with partners from the health and education sectors, civil society organizations (CSOs), local community-based organizations (CBOs), and the Network for the Defence of Sexual and Reproductive Rights (RDSR). The fairs and road shows created interactive spaces for youth and adults to access information on: SRHR and contraception; GBV prevention and reporting mechanisms; basic health services such as family planning, dental care, and HIV/AIDS testing and counseling.These efforts expanded community access points for SRH information and promoted good practices in SRH and GBV prevention. • Feminist Camp, on April 1112, Ipas hosted a Feminist Camp in Niassa Province to challenge gender norms and promote gender equality. The camp brought together 80 participants, including women from five districts: Sanga, Mandimba, Cuamba, Lichinga, and Chimbonila. The camp served as a platform for: critical discussions on SRHR, GBV, and access to safe abortion; sharing personal stories of resistance against patriarchal norms and building collective strategies for policy advocacy and womens empowerment. The highlight of the camp was the campfire story-sharing session, where women reflected on: resilience and self-love; societal beauty standards and gender expectations; intersectionality and the unique struggles faced by women of different backgrounds and this has fostered solidarity and strengthened feminist networks in Niassa Province. • In collaboration with the Monapo District Government, Ipas supported the organization of the first and second District Forums on Good Practices in Initiation Rites and Family Planning. These forums aimed to raise awareness among community stakeholders about SRHR and promote justice and equal opportunities for adolescents. A total of 378 community actors participated, including: 204 women and 174 men. Matrons, traditional birth attendants, community leaders, local chiefs, and post chiefs. Participants were sensitized and trained on: SRHR and contraceptive methods; Gender norms and GBV prevention; Community response strategies: Safe abortion as part of comprehensive reproductive health care.
The results below, contribute to Strategy objectives 2.2 Increased gender equality, including access to, and respect for, sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) of Strategy for Swedens development cooperation with Mozambique 20222026:
Objective 4: A national movement for SRHRled primarily by women and young peopledemands accountability from government leaders on SRHR and SGBV, and resists threats to progress
• During Y2, RDSR successfully organized two major events, reinforcing its advocacy for gender equality, SRHR, and safe abortion services. The first event was a commemorative Workshop for International Day of Action for Womens Health (May 28th), held in Maputo, that brought together representatives from government institutions, CSOs, health professionals, and advocacy groups. This workshop, held under the theme Gender Equality in Health Care aimed to reflect on gender equality in health care, focusing on gender-based violence (GBV) and sexual violence, assess progress and challenges in the implementation of the Maputo Protocol regarding womens rights in Mozambique, launch and discuss Ipas Mozambiques platform (Nurse Nina) for strengthening womens health services, and finally to recognize and honor key advocates in womens rights and SRHR. • Some key takeaways from this workshop were (i) increased awareness of gender disparities in healthcare and the importance of inclusive policies, (ii) strengthened commitment among stakeholders to advance womens health rights and (iii) advocacy strategies developed to address GBV and improve SRH service accessibility. • The second major event was the Workshop on International Safe Abortion Day (September 28th), held in Maputo in a hybrid format. This event brought together government officials, SRHR advocates, development partners (Canada, Sweden), and civil society representatives to discuss key challenges and progress in ensuring access to safe abortion services can exercise their rights and expanded public awareness campaigns to inform communities about abortion rights and services. It also addressed critical service delivery challenges, such as frequent stockouts of mifepristone and misoprostol due to USAID funding restrictions on abortion-related supplies, shortages of trained health care providers and the impact of conscientious objection, as well as the limiting service availability and stigma and misinformation which discourage women from seeking care. • The discussion also highlighted regional disparities, with Zambezia and Nampula experiencing severe shortages of abortion-related medications. While CSOs have intervened to fill these gaps, long-term, government-led solutions are necessary. Participants also emphasized the importance of engaging men and youth to challenge stigma and strengthen advocacy for policy reforms, particularly in supply chain management.
Establishment a grant-making mechanism Five organizations were selected through a rigorous two-phase evaluation process led by Ipas, followed by a detailed budget review to ensure alignment with project guidelines and the sustainability of planned interventions. Sida has reviewed the jurys recommendations and raised no objections to four organizations (Observatório das Mulheres, Lambda, AMODEFA, ACABE) and Rede DSR. Results related to the grant mechanism will be reported in the next CoP.
